F.why: Stepped ziggurat crown gives height at the head and reads from pitch 50; pale bodice over terracotta bell reads as a gown that flares and holds on the slim avatar.
F.fix: Slim the shoulder-width pale sleeve blocks, pull in a sash waist, add one more outward hem tier, and carry colour onto the back.

D.why: Sun-disc halo and fluted column pleats are the truest ancient sun-priestess, but the skirt is a straight column and the sleeves are broad.
D.fix: Splay the pleats into a tiered bell from the hip, slim the sleeves, and add more terracotta and green so it does not read as linen.

A.why: A very distinct stepped-stone outline with a sun crown, but a solid trapezoid with no arms, waist or feminine figure: a statue or cake.
A.fix: Carve a narrow shoulder, slim sleeves and a pinched waist, and keep the tiers only below the hip.

E.why: Sun-disc head is good, but the all-terracotta body collides with studded, and the split straight skirt reads as a tunic.
E.fix: Make pale stone dominant, build a closed bell skirt, and slim the sleeves.

B.why: Big terracotta shoulder cubes make the widest, brightest point the shoulders, so it reads as armour; the mitre leans.
B.fix: Remove the shoulder blocks for slim pale sleeves, straighten the crown, and widen the hem.

C.why: Dark grey sleeves and panels read as iron or a coat from above; straight skirt; the small diadem gives no height.
C.fix: Make the outline pale, slim the sleeves, add a bell skirt and a radiating crown; keep the gold trim.

notes: No candidate fully solves the sleeves: every set still uses shoulder-width arm blocks, so the brief's main flaw persists across the wave. The best next step would be to combine F's bell skirt and stepped crown with D's halo and pleats, plus slim sleeves and a sash waist. Backs are uniformly dark grey and read as iron; carry the palette round. Judged from sheet renders only, which are small, so fine trim is approximate.
